checkpoints: Raising the HTTP timeout only treats the symptom — the heavy task still blocks the web process
A background thread/Promise lives only in RAM, so any restart (deploy, crash, OOM) silently loses it
In the durable-queue model, the producer writes the job into Redis and returns immediately (202 + jobId) without waiting for processing to finish
A separate worker process pulls that job and processes it in the background, writing progress and result back into the store
Because state lives in the store rather than the web process's RAM, the client can poll job status anytime — even after the original request has closed
The job survives a worker restart because it gets picked back up from the durable queue rather than being lost
Decoupling lets workers scale independently of the web tier, and the queue's atomic operations let multiple workers safely share one queue
The trade-off cost: there is no synchronous result in the response — the client must switch to polling
Calling a timer function once at boot lives outside the application's lifecycle — you can't inject services into it, can't test it, and it isn't stopped cleanly on shutdown
A fixed-delay timer can only count an interval — it cannot express a calendar time point like "8 AM every day"
A real scheduler translates a cron expression into recurring trigger points, deciding only WHEN the job should fire
The scheduler is registered inside the application's lifecycle so the container manages it and cleans it up on shutdown
A registry holds a handle to every registered job so you can list next-run times, pause/resume, or delete a job — or add a new one at runtime with no redeploy
A queue is a fundamentally different concern: it decides WHO processes the work, adding guarantees the scheduler lacks — retries, durability, distributing work across workers
Production combines both: the cron callback only enqueues a job and returns immediately, so the scheduler is never blocked while a worker does the heavy work with retries
Conflating scheduler and queue — stuffing heavy work directly into the cron callback — is a classic design mistake

The charge handler calls the payment gateway and then records completion as two separate steps with no idempotency check between them, so a crash right after the gateway confirms the charge but before completion is recorded leaves the job marked failed and eligible for retry.

When BullMQ retries that crashed job, it re-runs the charge from the top with no guard against a prior successful charge, billing the customer a second time for real money — this is the most severe finding because it is a real-money incident, not just a data or logging bug.

Idempotency is achieved by using the payment id as the job id (already done) plus a check against previously processed payments before calling the gateway, or by passing an idempotency key to the gateway itself, so a rerun returns the original receipt instead of charging again.
The `onFailed` handler has no check on `job.attemptsMade` against the configured max attempts, so it runs — and pushes to the dead-letter queue — on every failed attempt, not only the final one.

Failing on attempt 1 or attempt 2 is expected behavior since a retry is still coming; treating every such transient failure as a dead-letter write produces duplicate dead-letter entries and false alerts for jobs that may still succeed.
The fix for that guard is a check such as `job.attemptsMade >= (job.opts.attempts ?? 1)` before calling `dlqQueue.add`, so only the truly exhausted job is written to the dead-letter queue.

`removeOnFail: true` makes BullMQ discard the job's stored data as soon as it is marked failed, so by the time `onFailed` runs on the final failure, `job.data` may already be gone — the dead-letter entry ends up empty or is never written at all, silently losing exactly the data ops needs most.
The fix for that retention gap is `removeOnFail: false` (or a bounded retention window), since the entire purpose of the `onFailed` handler is to still be able to read the job's data when it fires.

A correct severity ranking places the double-charge first because it is a real-money incident, the lost dead-letter data second because it silently destroys the record ops relies on, and the missing attempts guard last because it only produces noisy duplicate alerts rather than data loss or financial harm.

Correct verification would show a forced-fail job producing exactly one dead-letter entry written only after the final attempt, a simulated crash between the charge and completion steps producing exactly one charge after retry, and the dead-letter count staying flat while jobs are simply retrying as designed.

CPU sitting near 0% while a large backlog barely drains is the signature of an I/O-bound workload, not a CPU-bound one — each job spends nearly all its wall-clock time parked on an `await` for a network round-trip rather than doing computation.

At `concurrency: 1`, a BullMQ worker only ever has one job in flight, so the per-job network latency accumulates serially across the whole backlog — total drain time is roughly job count multiplied by per-job latency.

Raising worker concurrency lets multiple jobs be in flight on the same single-threaded event loop at once: while job A is suspended awaiting its I/O call, the loop is free to start job B's request, then job C's, so N one-second I/O waits overlap and finish in roughly one second instead of N seconds.

The speedup comes purely from interleaving idle wait time, not from added CPU parallelism — which is why the same change would not help, and could even hurt, a CPU-bound job like image resizing or hashing, since that work actually occupies the single JS thread instead of waiting on I/O.

Concurrency has a real ceiling set by downstream resources: pushing it past the size of a connection pool (database or SMTP) just queues the extra jobs waiting for a free connection, so real throughput caps at the pool size no matter how high concurrency is configured.

Pushing concurrency past a downstream provider's rate quota manufactures failed requests such as HTTP 429s, and the retries triggered by those failures can eat up whatever throughput gain the higher concurrency produced.

A safe concurrency value is sized to roughly the minimum of the connection-pool size and available quota headroom, with a queue-level rate limiter (for example `limiter: { max, duration }`) enforcing the hard quota explicitly instead of letting workers discover it by failing.

The right way to size concurrency is empirical rather than guessed: measure drain time and queue stats at several concurrency values, watch for connection-wait time and error responses as concurrency rises, and stop increasing at the knee of the curve where throughput stops improving and errors start climbing.

A `@Cron` callback that both decides when to run and performs the multi-minute work itself ties the trigger loop to the payload of that work — the two responsibilities live in one method and one process.

Node's event loop is single-threaded, so a CPU-bound loop like aggregating ~2M orders occupies the same thread that every other registered `@Cron`/`@Interval` in that process depends on to fire; while it runs, sibling schedules like a 5-second heartbeat cannot tick and either fire late or get skipped entirely.

The computed result of an inline aggregation exists only as a local variable in that one method invocation, with no durable record anywhere that the aggregation is even in progress — a process shutdown (SIGTERM from a deploy) discards it completely, and nothing knows to retry because no persisted state ever said the job existed.

The fix is to split scheduling from processing: the `@Cron` callback should do nothing but push a job onto a durable queue (e.g., BullMQ) and return immediately, taking milliseconds instead of minutes, so the event loop is freed and sibling schedules keep their cadence regardless of how long the real aggregation takes.

The actual aggregation logic moves into a separate worker/processor class that consumes the queue — because the job now lives in durable storage (Redis-backed queue) rather than in process memory, a mid-run process kill just leaves the job in a recoverable state instead of erasing it.

Stalled-job detection returns an interrupted job to the waiting state, and a configured `attempts`/`backoff` policy lets the worker retry it to completion on the next pickup, achieving restart-survival without any change to the scheduler side.

Keying the job id by the business period being processed (e.g., the date) makes the enqueue idempotent: a re-fired cron tick, a `SchedulerRegistry` restart, a retry, or a manual re-trigger all collapse onto the same job instead of producing duplicate or double-counted aggregations for the same night.

Decoupling scheduling from processing also lets the worker scale independently of the cron process — adding more worker instances handles a growing aggregation (e.g., month-end volume spikes) without touching how or when the job is triggered.

Simply speeding up the aggregation computation only shrinks the blocking and crash windows without removing either failure mode; a slow night can still delay sibling schedules and a crash at the wrong instant can still lose the run, whereas separating scheduling from processing eliminates both classes of bug structurally.

Verifying the fix requires checking both properties directly: confirming that sibling scheduled jobs keep firing on their normal cadence while a heavy aggregation runs, and separately killing the worker mid-aggregation to confirm the job is retried to completion with exactly one persisted result for that date.

Sketch of the flow: main queue → worker → transient failure retries with delay back onto the main queue up to N attempts → final failure → DLQ → dlq-worker/ops inspect and replay → back onto the main queue
Retry policy: 3 attempts with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s) plus jitter, so an entire fleet of failing workers doesn't retry in phase and pound the downstream at the same moment
Errors are classified before retrying: a permanent error (bad payload, 4xx) skips the retry loop and dead-letters immediately since retrying it only wastes attempts
A job enters the DLQ exactly once, at final failure (guard: attemptsMade >= max); intermediate failures only log a warning, which is the policy working as intended, not an incident

The dead-letter record must be kept with no auto-delete and must contain the original payload, last error, attempt count, and timestamps — enough for ops to diagnose and replay without log archaeology, unlike log-only which is a one-way stream you can't query or re-enqueue from
The operational surface needs a count/inspect endpoint, a size/TTL cap, and an alert when the DLQ crosses a threshold, since a silently growing DLQ means a lost incident
Replay pulls the record out and re-enqueues it onto the main queue, which is only safe because the handler is idempotent, so an original job that already ran halfway doesn't get double-executed
The ingest API has exactly one write action, bulk-enqueue (one shot, N jobs), returning immediately to confirm the batch was RECEIVED, not that it was SENT
A separate read endpoint exposes job counts by state so the campaign dashboard polls the queue, never the workers
The producer and worker fleet share exactly one thing — one shared durable queue — which IS the module boundary, with neither side needing to know the other's internals beyond the job's shape

Two scope-bound knobs: concurrency (C) interleaves jobs waiting on I/O inside one process — since sending email is I/O-bound, C can sit around 10-50, but is still capped from above by the connection pool or how many downstream connections are allowed; worker-process count (N) scales horizontally, and the atomic fetch mechanism guarantees each job lands on exactly one worker, so adding workers is safe by construction with no hand-rolled de-duplication logic

C and N multiply with each other (N×C potential in-flight jobs), so neither knob alone protects the SMTP quota — that's why the rate limiter set at the QUEUE level, not concurrency, is the single global ceiling (roughly 50 jobs/sec across the whole shared queue) keeping throughput shaped to the quota regardless of fleet size, and without it every scale-out event rediscovers the quota as a 429 storm plus retries

The lock TTL is budgeted beyond the worst-case job duration, extending the lock inside the handler for long batch jobs, so a healthy long-running job isn't mistaken by another worker for stalled and re-delivered
Graceful shutdown closes the worker at the right moment on deploy so in-flight jobs get to finish instead of being cut off and replayed

Delivery still sits on the at-least-once floor since no mechanism fully erases the chance of a replay, so each send is keyed idempotently by (campaignId, recipient) — good design makes duplicates rare, and idempotency makes that rare duplicate completely harmless

Identifies that in this scenario duplication originates on the producer/enqueue side: with a default enqueue, every `add` call spawns a brand-new job, so each client network retry or user double-click creates its own separate job.
States the producer-side fix: set `jobId` to a stable business identifier (e.g. `videoId`) so BullMQ recognizes every `add` with the same `jobId` as the same job and skips the duplicate.

Explains why the dedupe key must be a stable business id rather than a freshly-minted UUID per request — a per-request UUID would make every retry look like a different job and defeat dedupe instantly.

Identifies a second, independent layer of duplication risk: the queue only guarantees at-least-once delivery, so a stalled or failed job can be re-run by the system itself even with perfect producer-side dedupe.
Concludes that because of at-least-once delivery, the compress handler itself must be idempotent so a queue-triggered re-run still produces exactly one result.
Describes a concrete verification step: POSTing the same `videoId` twice returns the same `jobId`, and the worker's "processing" log line appears exactly once.
Describes a second verification step: after processing, the job's final state/result is a single one, confirming no double-processing actually happened.
Two separate bugs require two separate fixes: the timezone bug and the overlap bug.

Timezone bug root cause: a cron expression is evaluated against the scheduler's own clock, not the business's clock, so on a UTC container `0 2 * * *` fires at 2 AM UTC (9 AM in Ho Chi Minh, GMT+7), matching the morning-traffic complaint; also worth ruling out a 6-field seconds-first cron whose fields silently shift meaning when a 5-field expression is copied from a different tool, since that produces the same "wrong time" symptom for an unrelated reason.

Timezone fix: attach an explicit timezone option to the schedule (e.g. `Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh`) so the scheduler compensates, or standardize the whole system on UTC and apply the GMT+7 offset deliberately in one place instead of leaving it implicit.

Overlap bug root cause: the purge's duration occasionally exceeds the period between triggers, so the next trigger fires while the previous run is still going, and two purges execute concurrently against the same rows.
Single-instance guard: an in-memory `isRunning` flag skips the colliding tick, but this guard stops working once the service scales to multiple replicas because each replica keeps its own memory.
Multi-node fix: a distributed lock held in a shared store like Redis (`SET key NX EX ttl`, or a Redlock-style scheme), so whichever node acquires the lock runs the tick and the others skip it.
Lock hygiene: the lock must be released in a `finally` block, otherwise a purge that throws partway through leaves the lock held until its TTL expires, silently skipping ticks.
Optional throughput practice: keep the cron callback itself light by enqueuing the purge and returning immediately, so a slow purge can't block the scheduler's own clock.
Cron carries calendar semantics: the expression names actual time points and the scheduler re-anchors to the calendar on every trigger, right whenever the wall-clock moment genuinely matters.

Interval is a fixed delay measured from the previous run — right for a steady beat (heartbeat, cache refresh) where no calendar point matters, but each cycle's start slips by however long the handler itself takes; drift accumulates so interval can never express "at 2 AM", and picking it for a calendar-anchored job is a semantic bug that slowly wanders off the intended time.
Runtime-editable schedules add a new capability over a build-time static declaration: a registry lets admins add/stop/start jobs at runtime without redeploying.
New failure mode this introduces: that registry lives only in-memory, so a single restart wipes every dynamically added schedule.

Production fix: persist the schedule definitions in a database and re-register every active one during application bootstrap, or pick a store-backed scheduler (Hangfire, asynq) whose job definitions live in Redis and survive restarts and rolling deploys automatically.
Nuance: stop/pause keeps the job in the registry (resumable) while delete removes it permanently, so an admin's "disable" action should map to pause, not delete.
